introduction-the-precursor-to-ebpf.core: Before eBPF matured, SystemTap (Red Hat, around 2005) gave Linux dynamic tracing. You write scripts in a probe language, SystemTap translates them to C, compiles a kernel module and loads it to instrument kernel and user functions. It's powerful and still used on older enterprise kernels (RHEL 6 and 7), but it needs kernel debuginfo and a compiler, and loads real modules. Its ideas (probes, tapsets, aggregates) shaped bpftrace.

first_principles.problem: A RHEL 7 production system lacks modern eBPF support, but the team needs to trace kernel function latency.
truths: Dynamic tracing needs code in the kernel.

analogy.title: An older, heavier diagnostic machine
analogy.story: It does the job before the portable modern device existed, but needs more setup and care.
analogy.breaks: Old machines are safe once set up; kernel modules can crash the system if buggy.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Traces file opens on an older kernel.

code.text:
# stap -e 'probe syscall.openat { printf("%s(%d) %s\n", execname(), pid(), filename) }' -c 'cat /etc/hostname'
# requires: yum install systemtap kernel-devel-$(uname -r) kernel-debuginfo-$(uname -r)

check.q: Why is eBPF generally preferred over SystemTap on modern kernels?
check.a: eBPF programs are verified and JIT-compiled without building kernel modules or needing debuginfo, so they're safer and easier to deploy.

architecture-the-translation-loop.core: SystemTap runs in five passes. (1) Parse the script, (2) elaborate by resolving probe points and tapset symbols using debuginfo, (3) translate to C, (4) compile into a kernel module (stap_XXXX.ko) against kernel headers, (5) load the module with staprun, collect output and unload on exit. Compiled modules can be cached or cross-compiled and shipped to hosts without compilers using stap -p4 and staprun.

first_principles.problem: Production hosts can't have compilers installed, but the team needs SystemTap tracing.

analogy.title: Translating and printing a manual before delivery
analogy.story: Write it in one language, translate, print and bind it, then deliver the finished booklet to sites without printers.
analogy.breaks: Manuals don't depend on exact site details; modules must match the exact kernel version.

code.text:
# on build host with debuginfo
stap -r 3.10.0-1160.el7.x86_64 -p4 -m iolat iolat.stp     # → iolat.ko
scp iolat.ko prod01:/tmp/
# on production host (no compiler)
staprun /tmp/iolat.ko

check.q: What tool loads a precompiled SystemTap module on a host without a compiler?

syntax-the-probe-language.core: SystemTap scripts are made of probes and handlers: probe <point> { statements }. Points include kernel.function("vfs_read"), kernel.function("...").return, syscall.*, process("/path").function("name"), timer.s(1), begin and end. Handlers use built-ins (execname(), pid(), tid(), gettimeofday_us()), $variables for context (function arguments via debuginfo, $return), global associative arrays and statistical aggregates (<<< with @count, @avg, @hist_log).

first_principles.problem: The team needs per-process average latency of vfs_read on an older kernel.
truths: Entry and return probes bracket functions.
derivation: Store start time in **global array** keyed by tid.

analogy.title: A stopwatch at every door
analogy.story: Start the watch when someone enters a room, stop when they leave, and record the time in a ledger by name.
analogy.breaks: Ledgers grow forever; SystemTap arrays have size limits.

check.q: What does the <<< operator do in SystemTap?
check.a: Adds a value to a statistical aggregate, which can later be queried with @count, @avg, @max or histograms.

tapsets-the-standard-library.core: Tapsets are SystemTap's library of reusable probe aliases and functions (in /usr/share/systemtap/tapset). They expose stable, friendly names like syscall.open, ioblock.request, tcp.sendmsg, scheduler.cpu_on and vm.pagefault, with prepared variables (filename, size, devname) that hide kernel internals that change between versions. Example scripts in /usr/share/systemtap/examples cover many common investigations ready-made.

first_principles.problem: A script written for one kernel version breaks on another because internal function names changed.

analogy.title: A standard phrasebook
analogy.story: Instead of knowing local slang in every town, you use phrases that work everywhere.
analogy.breaks: Phrasebooks rarely change; tapsets evolve with SystemTap releases.

check.q: Why prefer tapset probes like syscall.open over raw kernel.function probes?
check.a: Tapsets provide stable, version-independent names and prepared variables, while internal function names can change between kernels.

safety-the-guru-mode.core: By default SystemTap enforces safety. Probe handlers have time and loop limits, memory access through $variables is checked, and embedded C code is forbidden. Guru mode (-g) lifts these restrictions, allowing embedded C (%{ ... %}), writes to kernel memory and modification of variables. It's useful for experiments or for patching a bug live as a band-aid, but a mistake can crash or corrupt the kernel, so reserve it for experts and test systems.

first_principles.problem: An engineer uses guru mode to modify a kernel variable in production and triggers a panic.
truths: Default mode is constrained for safety.

analogy.title: A maintenance override key
analogy.story: It lets a technician bypass safety interlocks, which is essential for rare repairs and dangerous if misused.
analogy.breaks: Override keys are physical; guru mode is just a flag.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows the boundary between observe and modify.

code.text:
# safe mode: read-only observation
stap -e 'probe kernel.function("tcp_retransmit_skb") { printf("%s\n", execname()) }'
# guru mode: embedded C, writes allowed — dangerous
# stap -g -e 'probe kernel.function("foo") { $flag = 0 }'

check.q: What does SystemTap guru mode allow that default mode doesn't?
check.a: Embedded C code and writing to kernel memory/variables, bypassing the default safety restrictions.
